newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey plans 55 small power plants in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Turkey plans 55 small power plants in 1997.

text.p: Turkey, facing energy shortages, is planning to open local tenders to have 44 more hydraulic power plants built in addition to 11 for which it invited tenders on Tuesday, an energy official said on Thursday.
"We will build those plants on the build-operate-transfer (BOT) model," said Mehmet Koyuncu, power affairs director at the energy ministry.
"Tenders have already been put out for the first 11 of them and those for the remaining 44 will be tendered later," he told Reuters, but did not say when.
He said the plants would be small-size production units which local contractors can build in four years on average.
Energy Minister Recai Kutan said Turkey's power demand would have risen by 12 percent this year, up from earlier estimates of eight percent, due to increasing number of industrial factories.
Turkey has a power generation capacity of 105 billion kiloWatt-hours (kWh) and is expected to produce 93.1 billion kWh against a demand of 97.5 billion.
It began importing electricity from Iran to make up for shortfall in supply and talks on imports from Georgia and Bulgaria are underway.

The BOT model, devised in the 1980s to finance big infrastructure projects through foreign-led consortia, hit bureaucratic snags after the constitutional court ruled that their finances should be inspected by the Council of State, which has delayed several big projects for years.
The government earlier this year introduced another model, called build-operate (BO), only for thermal power plants to encourage industrial plants to build their own power plants.
Officials said the 11 initial power plants would have a total established capacity of 2,688 MegaWatts (MW) and produce 9.29 billion kWh a year when completed.
Koyuncu did not say how much the remaining 44 plants were planned to produce.
Kutan said the government would break the ground for a 1,400-MW, 9.5-billion kWh gas-fired power plant near the industrial city of Bursa in the next two weeks.
He said the plant, to be built by a consortium led by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, would cost about $550 million and be completed in two-and-a-half years.
